description: AvenGuarde is a multidisciplinary team from Uzbekistan tackling NASA's "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars" challenge. Led by a published spatial data scholar with experience in satellite research and ML, our team brings together expertise in spatial analysis, full-stack software development, UI/UX design, and compelling science communication.
summary: Before a crew or a rover goes to the Moon or Mars, the mission is tested on Earth, at “analog” sites such as Iceland or the Atacama Desert. There is no shared measure of how close a site is to its target. Terrestrial Analog Finder is an open-source search engine that adds one. You pick a target: one of nine NASA Artemis III candidate landing regions at the lunar south pole, one of six Mars Exploration Zones, or an area you draw yourself. The engine compares it with all 3.2 million six-kilometre squares of Earth’s ice-free land on 12 to 13 measures of terrain, temperature and rock chemistry. It returns a ranked map of Earth, a list of sites, and for each site what matches and what does not. Every result is tested against 1,000 random patches. Without being given any list of analog sites, it ranks the Atacama, the Altiplano and the Qaidam basin far above chance, and it finds the best ground in Central Asia in the high Pamir. The results also show its limits: no ice-free place on Earth is cold enough to represent the lunar south pole, and none of the targets scores significantly above chance.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Terrestrial Analog Finder is a search engine for Earth analogs. You choose a target on the Moon or Mars, and it ranks all of Earth’s ice-free land by how alike it is to that target.
The built-in targets are NASA’s own: the nine candidate landing regions NASA published for Artemis III at the lunar south pole (October 2024), and six Exploration Zones proposed at NASA’s 2015 workshop on human landing sites on Mars (Jezero, Gale, Gusev, Meridiani Planum, Deuteronilus Mensae and Erebus Montes). A user can also draw a custom area.
Each search returns:
a map of Earth, coloured from most alike to least;
a list of sites: groups of neighbouring squares inside Earth’s best 1%;
for every site, each measure with its gap in real units, sorted into three lists: what matches, what fails, and what no place on Earth can offer;
a test of the best match against chance.

HOW IT WORKS
Collect. Open maps of height, temperature and rock for three worlds. Moon: LOLA elevation and Diviner temperature from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, and chemistry from the Lunar Prospector gamma-ray spectrometer. Mars: MOLA elevation from Mars Global Surveyor blended with HRSC from ESA’s Mars Express, and TES data from Mars Global Surveyor. Earth: ETOPO 2022 elevation, MODIS land surface temperature from Terra and Aqua, and the GLiM rock map.
Grid. Each world is cut into equal-area squares about 6 km across (HEALPix), so the poles are not stretched.
Measure. Every square gets the same numbers, at the same physical scale on all three worlds. Eight describe terrain: slope, roughness at four scales, ridge-or-valley position at two scales, and how much sky is open. Two or three describe temperature: the average, the day-night swing, and on Mars the seasonal swing. Two describe rock: silica and iron oxide. That is 12 measures for Earth-Moon and 13 for Earth-Mars.
Compare. Every measure is put on one 0-to-1 scale shared by Earth and the target world, so 7 degrees of slope means the same everywhere. Related measures are de-correlated so they are not counted twice. A square’s score is its mean distance to every square of the target.
Rank and check. Earth is sorted from most alike to least. The best match is then tested against 1,000 random patches of the same size and latitude on the target world. As a control, a patch of the Atacama Desert is given to the engine as if it were a target: Earth must match it far better than chance, and under the main ranking it does (p = 0.001).

BACKGROUND
The idea of finding terrestrial analogues for planetary exploration is not new. This project builds on existing methods, such as the dissimilarity index of Meyer and Pebesma (2021), to compare environments across different regions. Its contribution is bringing these methods together in one tool that searches Earth’s ice-free land using 12–13 environmental and geological measures. It also tests the results against 1,000 random patches on the Moon or Mars to determine whether the matches are better than chance.

RESULTS
We never gave the engine a list of analog sites. Afterwards we checked where well-known analog regions land. By chance, 1% of any region would fall inside Earth’s best 1%. For the nine lunar regions (median), 69% of the Qaidam basin falls inside it, 64% of the Atacama and Altiplano, and 25% of Hawaii’s Big Island around Mauna Loa. The Antarctic Dry Valleys are at 2% and Iceland at 0%.
For Jezero crater on Mars, the closest ground on Earth is the high Altiplano at the edge of the Atacama, one of the most studied Mars analogs.
A local example: for Malapert Massif at the lunar south pole, the closest ground in Central Asia is in the high Pamir, inside Earth’s best 0.01%. Tashkent itself ranks at 38%.

WHERE THE ANALOGY BREAKS
The challenge asks where the analogy breaks down, so the tool prints it for every site.
None of the 15 NASA targets passes the chance test. Earth’s closest ground is still far, mainly in temperature: the lunar south-pole regions are 50 to 105 kelvin colder than the coldest ice-free ground on Earth, and their day-night swing is about four times larger. A site can be right for testing a rover and wrong for testing survival of a lunar night.
One square is 6 km across. The tool points to regions, not to rocks or soil.
Mars temperatures are modelled from TES inputs, not measured. Earth’s rock chemistry is a lookup by rock class.
No place on Earth copies lunar or Martian gravity, air pressure, radiation or day length.
Iceland’s low rank does not make it a bad training site. It teaches geology up close; we measure 6 km squares.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
A 2014 review of analog sites (Preston & Dartnell) says “there are no clearly defined and followed criteria with which to evaluate them.” The tool adds three things that are missing: a common score, a check against chance, and stated limits. Mission planners and field teams can see which parts of a rehearsal will transfer to the target and which will not. Any country can read its own closest ground on the maps. A new target is one more run of the same code. The tool adds a measure to expert choice. It does not replace it.

WHAT IS CREATIVE
It starts from the target and searches the whole planet, where the usual approach starts from famous sites.
Earth is not divided into regions in advance. Every square is scored, so a valley comes out valley-shaped.
Every score ships with its chance baseline, and results that are not significant are kept and shown.
The catalogue of known analog sites is read only after a run, never to tune the method.

TOOLS
Python 3.11 with NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, astropy-healpix and jsonschema. FastAPI and Uvicorn for the web API. Google Earth Engine for one MODIS albedo export. Our own Python port of the KRC one-dimensional thermal model for Mars surface temperature. Git and GitHub. The live tool is at https://avenguarde.eengineer.net/. The code is open source under the MIT licence, and the code and every result are at https://github.com/Sherozbek2805/avenguarde.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Fairness between worlds (equal-area squares, the same physical scale, one shared scale per measure). Double counting of related measures. Whether a match beats chance. Data quality: rock chemistry is the weakest measure on both the Moon and Earth, and we say so. Repeatability: fixed random seed, written tests, and a log of every method decision.
